rejected.title: Newton's third law
card: Forces come in pairs. If object A exerts a force on object B, then B exerts a force on A at the same time.
The two forces in a pair are equal in size, opposite in direction and of the same type, such as both contact forces or both gravitational.
The two forces act on different objects. Because of this, they never cancel each other out.
The pair stays equal whatever the objects are like. It holds if one object is far heavier than the other, and whether each is still or moving.
rejected.remember: Every force has a partner of equal size and opposite direction, acting on the other object.

a.q: A skateboarder pushes on a wall with a force of 60 N to the right. What is the partner force?
opts: The wall pushes the skateboarder with 60 N to the left
The wall pushes the skateboarder with 60 N to the right
The skateboarder's weight pulls down on the skateboarder
The wall pushes the skateboarder with less than 60 N
a.why: The partner force acts on the other object, so the wall pushes on the skateboarder. It is equal in size and opposite in direction, so 60 N to the left. A force to the right would not be opposite to the skateboarder's push.
a.clue: Check each option against all three features of a pair.

b.q: A moving truck hits a parked car and pushes on it with 5000 N. What size is the force the car exerts on the truck?
opts: 5000 N, as the pair forces are equal in size
Less than 5000 N, as the car has less mass
More than 5000 N, as the car is damaged more
Zero, as the car was parked before the crash
b.why: The car's push on the truck is the partner of the truck's push on the car, so it is also 5000 N. The pair stays equal even though the truck is heavier and the car was still. Answering less than 5000 N mixes up the forces with their effects on each object.
b.clue: Think about what the third law says a pair depends on.

draft.title: Newton's third law
card: Forces come in pairs. If object A exerts a force on object B, then B exerts a force on A at the same time.
The two forces in a pair are equal in size, opposite in direction and of the same type, such as both contact forces or both gravitational.
The two forces act on different objects. Because of this, they never cancel each other out.
Equal forces do not mean equal accelerations. Each object's acceleration depends on the net force on it and on its own mass.
draft.remember: Every force has a partner of equal size, opposite direction, acting on the other object.

a.q: A skateboarder pushes on a wall with a force of 60 N to the right. What is the partner force?
opts: The wall pushes the skateboarder with 60 N to the left
The wall pushes the skateboarder with 60 N to the right
The skateboarder's weight pulls down on the skateboarder
The wall pushes the skateboarder with less than 60 N
a.why: The partner force acts on the other object, so the wall pushes on the skateboarder. It is equal in size and opposite in direction, so 60 N to the left. A force to the right would not be opposite to the skateboarder's push.
a.clue: The partner acts on the other object, in the opposite direction.

b.q: A tug of war rope is pulled by Ava and Ben. Ava pulls Ben with 300 N. Ben is dragged forward. What is the size of the force Ben exerts on Ava?
opts: 300 N, because the pair forces are always equal
More than 300 N, because Ben is moving towards Ava
Less than 300 N, because Ava is the one pulling
Zero, because Ben is only being dragged along
b.why: The force Ben exerts on Ava is the partner of the force Ava exerts on Ben, so it is also 300 N. Ben accelerates because of the net force on him, which includes other forces such as friction. It does not happen because the pair forces are unequal.
b.clue: Movement does not change the size of a pair of forces.

a.best: The wall pushes the skateboarder with 60 N to the left

b.best: 300 N, because the pair forces are always equal

problems.detail: In a tug of war Ava and Ben pull on the rope, not directly on each other, so 'Ava pulls Ben' and 'the force Ben exerts on Ava' blur two separate force pairs (Ava–rope and rope–Ben). The answer is 300 N only if the rope is treated as a light connector. Rewording to a direct push, or naming the rope pairs, would avoid teaching a muddled pairing.
The fourth bullet explains that acceleration depends on net force and mass. That is Newton's second law (point 3), explained here rather than only mentioned.
The clue ('acts on the other object, in the opposite direction') rules out every option except the right one, so it gives the answer away.
The clue ('Movement does not change the size of a pair of forces') directly rules out the zero, more and less options, so it gives the answer away.
